name: Medallion lakehouse
description:
A lakehouse organizes data on cheap object storage in an open table format, layered as bronze (raw, append-only, as-ingested), silver (cleaned, conformed, deduplicated), and gold (business-level aggregates and marts). The table format — Iceberg, Delta, or Hudi — is what turns a pile of Parquet files into real tables: ACID transactions, schema evolution, time travel, and hidden partitioning, all readable by any engine that speaks the format.

The strategic bet is engine-independence. Because storage is open, you can run Spark for heavy transformation, Trino for interactive SQL, DuckDB for local work, and a warehouse's external tables — all against the same single copy of the data, with no vendor holding the bytes hostage. A catalog (the control plane for table metadata and, increasingly, access control) is the piece teams underestimate: pick it deliberately, because migrating catalogs later is far more painful than swapping query engines.

This is the architecture of choice when data is large, multi-modal (files, events, tables), or serves multiple compute paradigms — BI, ML training, and streaming from one platform. The trade-off is operational surface: compaction, snapshot expiry, small-file management, and catalog governance are your problem in a way they simply are not on Snowflake. Choose it for the flexibility, staff it accordingly.
when_to_use: Choose this when data volumes are large enough that warehouse storage pricing hurts, when ML and BI must share one platform, or when open formats are a strategic requirement (avoiding lock-in, multi-engine access, M&A-driven heterogeneity).
It is also the natural landing zone for semi-structured and file-based data that a warehouse handles awkwardly.
You want warehouse-grade reliability on open formats without vendor lock-in.
when_not_to_use: Skip it if your workload is pure SQL analytics at small-to-medium scale — the ELT stack (2) delivers the same outcome with a fraction of the operational burden.
A lakehouse without a platform engineer becomes a swamp with a table format.
Sub-second serving latencies also live elsewhere (8, 22).

hot_spots.title: Small files
hot_spots.detail: Streaming ingest without compaction litters the lake and slows every reader.

hot_spots.title: Silver contracts
hot_spots.detail: Loose cleansing rules turn silver into a second bronze nobody trusts.

hot_spots.title: Table maintenance
hot_spots.detail: Skipped compaction and vacuum jobs degrade queries and bloat storage.

hot_spots.title: Catalog gaps
hot_spots.detail: Unregistered tables become invisible datasets with no lineage or access control.

evolution.reason: Scale the lakehouse across domains with product ownership and contracts.
Replace scheduled refinement with continuous commits when consumers need minutes-fresh tables.

stages.name: Lake storage
stages.role: Durable, cheap object storage holding all table data and metadata files
stages.rationale: S3 is the reference implementation every lakehouse tool targets first — eleven-nines durability, mature lifecycle policies, and S3 Express One Zone when metadata latency matters. ADLS and GCS are the equivalent picks on their clouds (ADLS's hierarchical namespace helps some workloads); MinIO when data must stay on-prem or you need S3 semantics in a sovereign environment. The pick follows your cloud; the discipline that matters is bucket layout, lifecycle rules, and keeping one region as the source of truth.

stages.name: Table format
stages.role: Turn object storage into ACID tables: transactions, schema evolution, time travel
stages.rationale: Iceberg has won the neutrality war: Snowflake, Databricks, Trino, Spark, DuckDB, and every catalog vendor treat it as the interchange format, so it maximizes the engine-independence that justifies a lakehouse in the first place. Delta Lake is the right call inside a Databricks-centric shop — deepest integration, best tooling there, and UniForm narrows the interop gap. Hudi still leads for heavy upsert/CDC-write workloads at extreme scale; Paimon if your world is Flink-first streaming into the lake. Whatever you pick, budget for table maintenance: compaction and snapshot expiry are not optional.

stages.name: Catalog
stages.role: Control plane for table metadata, namespaces, and increasingly access policy
stages.rationale: Polaris implements the Iceberg REST catalog spec as an open, vendor-neutral project (with Snowflake offering a managed flavor), which keeps the catalog — the hardest layer to migrate later — unowned by any single engine. Unity Catalog is the automatic choice on Databricks and brings the most mature governance (lineage, row/column policies) if you accept the platform gravity. Glue is pragmatic for AWS-native, Athena/EMR-heavy shops; Lakekeeper is a strong lightweight Rust implementation of the same REST spec; Nessie adds git-like branching of the whole catalog, powerful for write-audit-publish workflows.

stages.name: Ingest
stages.role: Land source data into bronze: batch loads and streaming appends
stages.rationale: Spark remains the workhorse writer for lakehouse bronze — every table format's write path is best-tested under Spark, and it covers both bulk backfills and Structured Streaming appends from Kafka in one engine. Kafka (with Iceberg-aware connectors) is the transport when sources are event streams; dlt is the lighter pick for API/database batch sources writing Parquet or Iceberg directly without cluster overhead; Estuary Flow when you want managed CDC straight into the lake. Keep bronze append-only and as-raw-as-possible — reprocessing ability is the layer's entire value.

stages.name: Transform
stages.role: Refine bronze to silver to gold: cleansing, conformance, business aggregates
stages.rationale: Spark handles the bronze-to-silver work that is genuinely procedural — deduplication, complex parsing, MERGE-heavy CDC application, ML feature prep — at any scale. But run silver-to-gold as SQL under dbt (against Spark, Trino, or Databricks SQL) so analysts own the business layer with tests and lineage; the healthiest lakehouses split exactly along that line. SQLMesh is the alternative modelling layer with stronger incremental semantics; pure-Trino transformation works when everything is expressible in SQL and you want one less engine.

stages.name: Query
stages.role: Interactive SQL over silver and gold for BI and ad-hoc analysis
stages.rationale: Trino is the open, engine-independent query layer the architecture promises — fast federated SQL over Iceberg with a huge connector ecosystem, self-hosted or via managed offerings. Databricks SQL wins when you are already on Databricks: Photon performance plus Unity governance with zero extra moving parts. DuckDB is a genuinely great Iceberg/Parquet reader for local and small-scale analysis; Snowflake's Iceberg external tables let warehouse users query the lake without another engine; Dremio bundles query plus semantic layer if you want a product rather than a component.
